subtype: Approach: making a range and giving reasons [Action]
passage:
Deepak: Hi Anjali! HR has approved the offer: 9.5 lakh a year. Happy to talk through it.
Anjali: Thank you, I'm excited! Based on my project results and my cloud certifications, I was hoping for something between 10.5 and 11.5.
Anjali: The forecasting model I built cut stock-outs by a fifth at my last company, and I passed both certification exams this year.
Deepak: That's useful context. Let me check with the team.
Deepak: We can do 10.6. Can you confirm?
Anjali: 10.6 works for me. Thank you for hearing me out 🙂
Deepak: Great! The letter comes tomorrow 🎉

qa.q: What figure did Deepak offer after checking with the team?
qa.a: Deepak said, "We can do 10.6."

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt while waiting for Deepak to check with the team?
qa.a: Anjali was probably hopeful but nervous, having asked for more than the first offer.

qa.q: What else could Anjali ask about after agreeing on the figure, and why?
qa.a: Anjali could ask when the first pay review takes place, because it shows how the project results can be recognised again later.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Anjali's message?
qa.a: Deepak likely finds it clear and reasonable, since it gave a range and specific reasons that were easy to take back to the team.

grounding: Illustrates asking for a range slightly above the target, backed by project results and certifications, and accepting a counter within that range.

passage: On the terrace above his family's hardware shop in a small town, Chetan had one online post open on his phone: a stranger claiming to have joined a company at triple the usual pay. Phone to his ear, he told Nirmala, the recruiter, "I want three times what you offered." A pause. "That's far beyond what this role pays," Nirmala said politely. "I don't think we can go further. Thank you for your time." The line clicked. Chetan sat among the rolls of wire, stunned. Two weeks passed and no other offer came. He wrote back to ask about the original figure. Nirmala replied that the role was still open, but the number on offer now was lower than before.

qa.q: What was Chetan's demand based on?
qa.a: Chetan based his demand on one online post.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel after the call ended?
qa.a: Chetan was stunned and probably embarrassed, sitting among the rolls of wire.

qa.q: What could Chetan have done instead of relying on the post, and why?
qa.a: Chetan could have checked several sources and asked peers about typical pay for the role, because one unusual case is a poor guide to the market.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have seen Chetan's demand?
qa.a: Nirmala probably saw it as unrealistic and ended the talk politely, and the goodwill was harder to regain afterwards.

grounding: Illustrates demanding a figure far above the market based on one unusual post, so the recruiter ends the discussion and the later ask is at a lower figure.

subtype: Approach: reviewing the outcome and preparing for the next round [Revision]
passage: Ishrat settled slightly below her target and signed the letter before six o'clock, the deadline the company had set. On the train home she typed a note on her phone. What worked: giving a range, and quoting the two client projects. What didn't: I forgot to ask about a joining bonus. The next morning she asked her manager, Vishal, for fifteen minutes and put a review date in the calendar: the first week of October. Then she listed three results to measure by then: report turnaround time, error rate, and number of clients supported. "Next time I ask, I'll bring the numbers," she wrote at the bottom of the note.

qa.q: What review date did Ishrat set with Vishal?
qa.a: Ishrat put a review date in the calendar for the first week of October.

qa.q: How does Ishrat probably feel about settling below her target?
qa.a: Ishrat is probably a little disappointed but determined to do better next time.

qa.q: What else could Ishrat do until the review, and why?
qa.a: Ishrat could update her list of results every month, because up-to-date numbers are easier to present than recollections.

qa.q: How might Vishal see the request for a review date?
qa.a: Vishal probably sees it as a sign of initiative and may be more ready to listen when the date arrives.

grounding: Illustrates noting what worked after settling slightly below target, setting a review date with the manager and planning measurable results for a stronger request.

subtype: Approach: asking for a review after a raise is refused [Revision]
passage: The finance head had frozen raises for the year, and Yogesh said so with an apologetic face. Vaibhav had half expected the answer, and had a second question ready. "Could we write down a date to look at it again, and what you'd want to see from me by then?" That evening Yogesh emailed: review in March, and three targets, which were two client launches on time, one process document, and mentoring the new hire. Vaibhav pinned the email above his desk. Six months later he brought a one-page sheet: all three targets met, with dates. "I'd like to reopen the raise," he said. Yogesh read it and nodded. "I can take this to finance with a straight face."

qa.q: For which month did the review get scheduled?
qa.a: The review was scheduled for March.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when hearing that raises were frozen?
qa.a: Vaibhav had half expected it, so he was disappointed but steady, with a second question ready.

qa.q: What else could Vaibhav do during the six months, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav could ask Yogesh for feedback at the halfway point, because it shows whether the targets are on track before the review.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have seen Vaibhav's request for a written review date?
qa.a: Yogesh probably felt relieved that Vaibhav accepted the news constructively, and could support the raise more easily with clear targets.

grounding: Illustrates asking for a written review date and clear targets when a raise is refused, then reopening the talk six months later with results.

subtype: Approach: gathering specific examples before speaking [Thinking]
passage: I'm Hafsa, and I sit next to Nikhil's desk. Before he spoke to Tanish last Thursday, I watched Nikhil open a notes file and type a list: three tasks handed in late this month, two changes pushed without tests. He wrote down the dates. Then he deleted the word "careless" from the top line and typed "what happened". Through the glass I heard: "Three tasks came in after their dates, and two changes went out untested. Help me understand what was going on." Tanish looked at the table for a moment and then began to talk. I can't say what Nikhil was thinking. But it looked as if he wanted the conversation to stay on the work.

qa.q: How many tasks were handed in late this month?
qa.a: Three tasks were handed in late this month.

qa.q: What might Nikhil have been feeling when deleting the word "careless"?
qa.a: Nikhil seems to have been concerned about being fair and wanted to avoid a label that would make Tanish defensive, though Hafsa can only guess.

qa.q: What else could Nikhil do in the talk, and why?
qa.a: Nikhil could ask Tanish what would make it easier to finish tasks and test changes, because the answer shows whether the problem is effort, skill or support.

qa.q: How might Tanish have felt hearing dates and facts instead of a label?
qa.a: Tanish was probably nervous but relieved to be asked about what happened, which makes it easier to answer honestly.

grounding: Illustrates a lead listing what actually happened, three late tasks and two untested changes, and avoiding labels so the talk stays on observable work.

subtype: Approach: root cause analysis with the junior [Thinking]
passage: In a private cabin at a software firm in Gurgaon, Vinita closed the door and began with a question, not a verdict. "Tasks have been slipping for three weeks. What's making them hard?" Manav stared into his coffee. "I don't really understand the codebase," he said. "The payment module. I've read it three times. I didn't want to keep asking, everyone seems so busy." Vinita nodded slowly. If effort were the problem, she thought, he'd be hiding, not reading the same module three times. She had come ready to talk about effort. Instead she saw a gap in support: no walkthrough, and nobody to ask. "Thank you for telling me. Let's fix the explaining, not you." She booked an hour for a walkthrough the next day.

qa.q: Which module did Manav say he found hard to understand?
qa.a: Manav said he found the payment module hard to understand.

qa.q: Why did Manav avoid asking for help?
qa.a: Manav was afraid of bothering people, since everyone seemed so busy.

qa.q: What else could Vinita do to support Manav, and why?
qa.a: Vinita could ask a teammate to be available for quick questions each day, because a small regular source of help makes it easier to ask.

qa.q: How might Manav have felt when Vinita said to fix the explaining, not him?
qa.a: Manav probably felt relieved and less ashamed, since the problem was named as a lack of support rather than a fault in him.

grounding: Illustrates a lead asking a junior in private what is making tasks hard and finding the problem is missing support, not effort.

subtype: Approach: setting small clear tasks with regular check-ins [Action]
passage:
Friday. Week two of the new way with Pankaj. Instead of "build the export module", I hand over "add the CSV header row; done when the test passes." Every day at 11:30 we sit together for ten minutes and look at what's finished. This week Pankaj completed six small pieces. On Wednesday I saw Pankaj grin when a test went green, a proper grin, not a polite one. It isn't perfect. The fourth piece had to be redone. But for the first time I can actually see progress, and so can Pankaj. Tomorrow's task is a little bigger: the date column. If that goes well, maybe two pieces at once by next week.

Aadhya

qa.q: How long is the daily review Aadhya holds with Pankaj?
qa.a: They sit together for ten minutes each day.

qa.q: How did Pankaj seem to feel when the test went green?
qa.a: Pankaj seemed pleased and more confident, showing a proper grin.

qa.q: What else could Aadhya do to keep the approach working, and why?
qa.a: Aadhya could ask Pankaj to write the acceptance criteria for the next piece, because it builds Pankaj's own sense of what done looks like.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see the new way of handing over work?
qa.a: Aadhya sees it as working though not perfect, because for the first time Aadhya can actually see progress, even with one piece redone.

grounding: Illustrates giving a junior smaller tasks with acceptance criteria and a daily ten-minute review so progress becomes visible and confidence grows.

passage: On the fourth-floor bay of the software firm, Shreya walked Himani over to Rishi's desk. "Himani, you know this codebase, and you never make anyone feel silly for asking. Could you pair with Rishi on Tuesdays and Thursdays?" Himani smiled. "Sure. Mornings?" Rishi looked relieved and a little shy. On the first Tuesday, Himani typed while Rishi watched, and then they switched. Himani showed how the team names branches, where the test folder lives, and which reviewer answers fastest. By the third week, Rishi had stopped sending Shreya the same three questions. Shreya's afternoons were quieter, and Rishi's tasks came in on time.

qa.q: On which days do Himani and Rishi pair?
qa.a: They pair on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

qa.q: How did Rishi feel when Himani agreed to pair?
qa.a: Rishi felt relieved and a little shy.

qa.q: What else could Shreya do to help the pairing work, and why?
qa.a: Shreya could check in with both after a month, because the pair may need to change the days or the topics as Rishi grows more confident.

qa.q: How might Himani feel about taking on the buddy role?
qa.a: Himani probably feels trusted and pleased to help, though it takes time out of Himani's own work.

grounding: Illustrates a lead assigning a friendly mid-level colleague to pair with a junior twice a week so the junior learns team habits faster and fewer explanations fall to the lead.

subtype: Approach: doing the junior's work quietly [Pitfall]
passage:
Tuesday, 1 am. Rewrote Sumeet's login code again after everyone left. Third time this month. The deadline is Friday, there's no time to explain, and explaining would take longer than just doing it. Sumeet doesn't know. He'll send the next ticket and we'll go around again. My neck aches and my eyes burn. Tomorrow I have to sit at stand-up and act as though everything's fine. I keep thinking he'll never learn what was wrong, because I've never told him. Maybe I should have said something in week one. Maybe next week. I can't see how long I can keep this up, and the code he writes hasn't changed at all.

Rukmini

qa.q: How many times this month has Rukmini rewritten Sumeet's code?
qa.a: It is the third time this month.

qa.q: How does Rukmini feel at 1 am after the rewrite?
qa.a: Rukmini feels exhausted and anxious, with an aching neck and burning eyes, and unsure how long this can continue.

qa.q: What could Rukmini do differently, and why?
qa.a: Rukmini could show Sumeet the changes in daytime and explain the reasons, because he cannot improve at what he never gets told about.

qa.q: How might Sumeet see the situation?
qa.a: Sumeet probably thinks the code is fine, since nobody has told him otherwise, and he does not know how much extra work Rukmini is doing.

grounding: Illustrates a lead rewriting a junior's code at night without telling him to meet deadlines, so he never learns and the lead burns out.

passage:
Day 1. At the Monday meeting, Vasudha, frustrated by three bugs, put the code on the big screen. "Vinita, line 42 again. Did you even run it?" Nobody laughed. Vinita's ears went red.

Day 8. In stand-up Vinita said only "fine" and asked no questions, though the comments on her ticket showed she was stuck.

Day 20. A customer reported a crash in a module Vinita had touched. The history showed a problem Vinita had noticed a week earlier and never mentioned. Two more bugs turned up in the same module that afternoon.

qa.q: Which line did Vasudha point out on the big screen?
qa.a: Vasudha pointed out line 42.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when the code was shown to the whole team?
qa.a: Vinita felt embarrassed and humiliated, as her ears going red suggests.

qa.q: What could Vasudha have done instead, and why?
qa.a: Vasudha could have spoken to Vinita privately about the bugs and asked what would help, because criticism in private keeps questions and honesty alive.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team have been affected?
qa.a: The rest of the team probably felt uneasy, worried they might be next, and less willing to admit their own mistakes.

grounding: Illustrates a frustrated lead pointing out mistakes in front of the team so the junior withdraws, stops asking questions and hides errors.
